title: From one student to many
goal: Represent several records with lists and dictionaries before building a table.
prerequisites: Complete the dictionary examples in Module 1.

cells.title: A list has positions
cells.explanation: A list stores values in order. Positions start at 0, so names[1] is the second value. A slice such as [0:2] includes positions 0 and 1 but excludes position 2. A negative position counts back from the end.
cells.code:
names = ["Amira", "Bilal", "Chloe", "Dana"]
print(names[0])
print(names[-1])
result = names[0:2]
print(result)

questions.prompt: What do the square brackets mean when names is first created?
questions.answer: They create a list containing four text values in order.

questions.prompt: What is printed by names[-1] and names[0:2]?
Why does [0:2] return two names rather than three?
questions.answer: The start position is included, but the stop position 2 is excluded.

cells.task: Select only Bilal and Chloe into result using one slice. Then append Ethan and print the new list length.
cells.hint: Start the slice at position 1 and stop before position 3.
cells.solution:
names = ["Amira", "Bilal", "Chloe", "Dana"]
result = names[1:3]
names.append("Ethan")
print(result)
print(len(names))
cells.solution_note: The slice returns Bilal and Chloe. append() adds a value at the end, so the full list now has five names.

check.prompt: Which expression selects the second value?
check.feedback: Positions start at 0, so the second value is at position 1.

cells.solution_verify:
assert result == ['Bilal', 'Chloe']
assert names[-1] == 'Ethan' and len(names) == 5
cells.watch: A single position returns one item; a slice returns a list, even if it contains one item.
cells.takeaway: I can predict list positions and slices.

cells.title: A dictionary of lists describes columns
cells.explanation: Now each dictionary value is a list. The keys describe future column names, and values at the same position belong to the same student. data["Age"] chooses a list; the second pair of brackets chooses an item inside that list.

questions.prompt: What is the type of data, and what is the type of data["Age"]?
questions.answer: data is a dictionary. data["Age"] is a list.

questions.prompt: Which student is described by position 1 in all three lists?
What can go wrong if you reorder only the names list?
questions.answer: Names could become paired with another student's age and campus. The lists must stay aligned by position.

cells.task: Change Chloe's age from 19 to 20 without changing the other ages. Print Chloe's name and updated age.
cells.hint: Chloe is at position 2 inside each list.
cells.solution_note: The age list becomes [20, 21, 20]. Updating one nested list position does not change the other positions.

check.feedback: The first brackets retrieve the Age list; the second retrieve its position 1.

cells.watch: Positions in lists are numbers; dictionary keys can be text. Do not swap their roles.
cells.takeaway: I can read a value from a dictionary containing lists.

cells.title: A list of dictionaries describes rows
cells.explanation: A second arrangement stores one dictionary per student inside a list. Each dictionary is a record, or row. rows[1] selects the second record; ["Name"] then selects a field within it. Both arrangements can later become a pandas DataFrame.

questions.prompt: What is stored in each element of rows?
questions.answer: One dictionary describing one student record.

questions.prompt: Why is the order of the brackets different from data["Name"][1] in the previous cell?
questions.answer: rows is organized as a list of records, so select the record first. data was organized as named columns, so select the column first.

cells.task: Add Dana, age 22, at Dubai as a fourth dictionary. Print the last student's name and the total record count.
cells.solution_note: Dana is the last record and there are four records. This arrangement keeps each student's fields together.

check.prompt: Which arrangement stores one dictionary per row?
check.feedback: A list of dictionaries groups each record's fields inside its own dictionary.

cells.watch: Count records with len(rows); len(rows[0]) counts fields in the first record.
cells.takeaway: I can tell column-oriented data from row-oriented records.

cells.title: Check lengths before making a table
cells.explanation: A rectangular table needs the same number of values in each plain list column. len() counts the values in a list. You can inspect all column lengths before constructing the DataFrame. A missing measurement still needs a position, often filled with None.

questions.answer: It compares two lengths and returns True or False. It does not assign a value.

questions.prompt: What happens to same_length if you remove the last age only?
questions.answer: It becomes False: there would be three names but only two ages.

questions.prompt: Why is adding a zero not always a good way to represent an unknown age?
questions.answer: Zero is a real numerical value. Using it could incorrectly suggest the student is zero years old and distort calculations.

cells.task: Add Dana to the Name list. Her age is unknown, so append None to Age. Confirm that the two lengths still match.
cells.hint: Append one value to each list; use None without quotes.
cells.solution:
data = {
    "Name": ["Amira", "Bilal", "Chloe"],
    "Age": [20, 21, 19]
}
data["Name"].append("Dana")
data["Age"].append(None)
same_length = len(data["Name"]) == len(data["Age"])
print(data)
print("Matching lengths:", same_length)
cells.solution_note: Both lists now contain four positions. None marks the missing age while preserving the row alignment.

check.prompt: What is needed for a DataFrame built from plain list columns?
options: All column lists must have equal length.
Each column must have a different length.
check.feedback: Plain list columns must have equal lengths. Indexed Series have separate alignment rules, introduced next.

cells.verify: assert lengths == {'Name': 3, 'Age': 3} and same_length is True
cells.solution_verify:
assert same_length is True and len(data['Name']) == 4
assert data['Age'][-1] is None
cells.watch: None is a missing-value marker here; "None" in quotes is ordinary text.
cells.takeaway: I can check whether list-based columns form a consistent table.
